name: GO Classes CS Test Series | C programming | Subject Wise Test 3

question.text:
Consider the following two blocks of code, which are contained in separate files:

main.c 

void foo(); 

int i = 0;
int main() {
    foo();
    return 0;
}

foo.c 

int i = 1;
void foo() {
    printf("%d", i);
}

What will happen when you attempt to compile, link, and run this code?

  1. It will fail to compile.
     
  2. It will fail to link.
     
  3. It will print "$0$".
     
  4. It will print "$1$".

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output?

#include <stdio.h>
int i = -12; /* global variable */
void myfunc(void)
{
    int i = -10;
    printf("%d\n", i);
}
void myfunc2(void)
{
    i = -10;
}
int main(void)
{
    printf("%d\n", i);
    myfunc();
    printf("%d\n", i);
    myfunc2();
    printf("%d\n", i);
}
  1. $-12$,
    $-10$,
    $-10$,
    $-10$
     
  2. $-12$,
    $-10$,
    $-12$,
    $-10$
     
  3. $-12$,
    $-12$,
    $-12$,
    $-10$
     
  4. $-12$,
    $-12$,
    $-12$,
    $-12$

You are given the following variable declarations of p and q:

/* Declaration */

double p = 25.50, q = 10.00;

Which of the following if statements will NOT print Yes?

Hint: Look carefully at the semicolons (;)

  1. if (p >= 30 && q < 30);
    printf("Yes");
  2. if (q == 25.00 || 10.00)
    printf("Yes");
  3. if (!p && q < 30)
    printf("Yes");
  4. if (p == 10.00 || q != 25.50)
    printf("Yes");

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output produced by this program?
 

int x = 0;
void swap(int x, int *y) {
    int temp = x;
    x = *y;
    * y = temp;
}
int main(void) {
    int x = 1;
    int y = 2;
    swap(x, &y);
    printf("x = %d y = %d \n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
  1. $x=1 \quad y=1$
     
  2. $x=1 \quad y=2$
     
  3. $x=2 \quad y=1$
     
  4. $x=2 \quad y=2$

Consider the following number line showing a specific range where the line is bold. Filled circles represent points that are included in the range, and hollow circles represent points that are not included.

 



Which one of the following conditions results in true if n is in the range shown and false otherwise?

  1. $\mathrm{n}>-7| | \mathrm{n}<3 \& \& \mathrm{n}==5 \& \& \mathrm{n}==7$
     
  2. $\mathrm{n}>-7| | \mathrm{n}<3| | \mathrm{n}==5| | \mathrm{n}==7$
     
  3. $\mathrm{n}>-7 \& \& \mathrm{n}<3 \& \& \mathrm{n}==5| | \mathrm{n}==7$
     
  4. $\mathrm{n}>-7 \& \& \mathrm{n}<3$ || $\mathrm{n}==5$ || $\mathrm{n}==7$

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output?
 

#include <stdio.h>
void swap(int* a, int* b, int* c)
{
    int* temp = c;
    * c = *b;
    * b = *a;
    * a = *temp;
}
int main(void)
{
    int x, y, z;
    x = 1;
    y = 2;
    z = 3;
    swap(&x, &y, &z);
    printf("x = %d y = %d z = %d\n", x, y, z);
}
  1. $x=3 \quad y=2 \quad z=1$
     
  2. $x=3 \quad y=2 \quad z=2$
     
  3. $x=1 \quad y=2 \quad z=3$
     
  4. $x=2 \quad y=1 \quad z=2$

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output?

#include<stdio.h>
void swap(int count, int A[], int B[])
{
    int i, temp;
    for (i = 0; i < count; ++i)
    {
        temp = A[i];
        A[i] = B[i];
        B[i] = temp;
    }
}
int main(void)
{
    int A[5] = {1, 6, 4, 5, 9};
    int B[5] = {2, 7, 11, 14, 3};
    int C[7] = {1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 2, 9};
    swap(3, A, B);
    swap(4, B, C);
    swap(5, A, C);
    printf("%d %d %d\n", A[3], B[4], C[5]);
    return;
}
  1.  $4\quad22\quad9$
     
  2.  $14\quad3\quad2$
     
  3.  $5\quad3\quad2$
     
  4.  $14\quad29\quad2$

Consider the following C code:

int x[2][3] = { {10, 20, 30}, {40, 50, 60} };
int *p = *(x + 1); 
printf("%d", *(p + 2));

What will be the output of the above program?
 

  1. $30$
     
  2. $50$
     
  3. $60$
     
  4. Segmentation fault

The following Cprogram compiles and runs without errors. What is the output the program produces?

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    char test_str[50] = "1010_fighting";
    char *str_ptr = &test_str[2];
    while (*str_ptr != '\0')
    {
        printf("%c", *(str_ptr++));
    }
}
  1. $0$_fighting
     
  2. $10$_fighting
     
  3. $1$
     
  4. $1010$_fighting

You compile and run the following C program. What is the output?

#include <stdio.h>
int i; /* global variable */
void plusplus(int i)
{
    i++;
}
int main(void)
{
    for (i = 0; i < 10; plusplus(i))
    {
    }
    printf("i = %d\n", i);
    return 0;
}
  1. i = $9$
     
  2. i = $10$
     
  3. i = $11$
     
  4. There will be an infinite loop.

What will be the output of the following program?

void g(int **x, int *y, int *z) {
    **x = 10;
    *x = z;
    printf("%d %d %d", **x, *y, *z);
}
void f(int *q, int n, int *p) {
    n = n + 2;
    *p = *p * *q;
    g(&q, &n, p);
}
int main() {
    int a = 7, b = 2;
    f(&a, b, &b);
}
  1. $14$  $4$  $14$
     
  2. $10$  $4$  $14$
     
  3. $14$  $2$  $14$
     
  4. $10$  $2$  $14$

Which of the following loops produces the same value for the variable x as the loop shown below?
 

int i, x = 0;
for(i = 0; i <= 100; ++i)
    x += i;
printf("x = %d \n", x); /* prints x = 5050 */

  1. int i = 0, x = 0;
while (i <= 100)
    x += i;
printf("x = %d\n", x);
  2. int i = 0, x = 0;
do {
    x += i;
} while (i <= 100);
++i;
printf("x = %d\n", x);
  3. int i = 0, x = 0;
while (i <= 100) {
    x += i++;
}
printf("x = %d\n", x);
  4. int i = 0, x = 0;
while (i <= 100) {
    x += ++i;
}
printf("x = %d\n", x);

The following program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output of the program?
 

#include<stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    int arr[5] = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10};
    int *ptr = arr;
    printf("%d ", *ptr + 1);
    printf("%d\n", *(ptr + 1));
}
  1. $44$
     
  2. $35$
     
  3. $34$
     
  4. $46$

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output?

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    int i = 3, j = 2;
    int x = (i++) * (--j);
    int y = -(--j);
    int z = (++i) * 5;
    printf("%d %d %d\n", x, y, z);
}
  1. $3$   $0$   $25$
     
  2. $3$   $-1$   $20$
     
  3. $6$   $-2$   $15$
     
  4. $4$   $-1$   $20$

Assume that the code fragment shown below is put in a complete C program that compiles and runs without errors. Further assume that when the program is running, the address of the variable named ptr is \(1000\) and the address of the variable named \(\mathbf{x}[\mathbf{0}]\) is \(1008\). After the code fragment executes, what is the value of *ptr?

int *ptr;
int x[3] = {1016, 1024, 1032};
ptr = x;
  1. $1000$
     
  2. $1008$
     
  3. $1016$
     
  4. $1024$

Consider the following C code snippet:

char *p = malloc(10);
if (x >= 10)
    free(p);
if (x < 11)
    free(p);

Which of the following combinations of x value and bug name correctly describes the dangerous behavior in this code?

  1. x = 9, Bug: Memory Leak
     
  2. x = 10, Bug: Double Free (i.e., the pointer p is freed twice)
     
  3. x = 11, Bug: Dangling Pointer
     
  4. x = 5, Bug: Invalid Allocation

The following Cprogram compiles and runs without error. What is the output?

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    int x = 10, y = 5;
    switch(x + y)
    {
        case 10: x += 5;
                 y += 5;
        case 15: x -= 5;
                 y += 5;
        case 5:  x += 5;
                 y += 5;
        default: x = 5;
                 y = 10;
    }
    printf("%d %d", x, y);
}
  1. $10$   $15$
     
  2. $10$   $5$
     
  3. $5$   $10$
     
  4. $15$   $20$

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output the program produces?

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    int test[3][2] = {{2, 3}, {4, 5}, {6, 7}};
    int i = 0, j = 0;
    printf("%d ", test[++i][j++]);
    printf("%d", test[i++][--j]);
}
  1. $3$  $0$
     
  2. $4$  $0$
     
  3. $4$  $3$
     
  4. $4$  $4$

What will be the output of this program? 

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    char string[10] = "abcdefgh", *p = string, ch;
    while (*p != '\0') {
        ch = *p++;
        *p++ = ch;
    }
    printf("%s\n", string);
    return 0;
}
  1. abcdefgh
     
  2. aacceegg
     
  3. bbcddffh
     
  4. None of the above

Given an incomplete C program shown below, which one of the following answer choices can NOT be a valid prototype for myfunc?

#include<stdio.h>
/* missing prototype */
int main(void)
{
    int result;
    int a[5][5] = {{1}};
    result = myfunc(a);
    printf("result = %i \n", result);
}
/* code for myfunc goes here */
  1. $int \quad myfunc (int \quad a[][5]);$
     
  2. $int \quad myfunc (int\quad a[5][]);$
     
  3. $int \quad myfunc (int\quad b[5][5]);$
     
  4. $int \quad myfunc (int\quad [5][5]);$

Consider the following C program:

struct Data {
    int x;
    int y;
};
int main() {
    struct Data d = {10, 20};
    struct Data *p = &d;
    printf("%d\n", *((int *)p + 1));
    return 0;
}

What will be the output of the program?

  1. $10$
     
  2. $20$
     
  3. Garbage value
     
  4. Compilation error

The following Cprogram compiles and runs without errors. What is the output produced by this program?
 

#include<stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    int a[] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    int *c;
    int *b = a;
    printf("%d ", *(b++));
    c = b;
    printf("%d ", ++(*c));
}
  1. $10\quad21$
     
  2. $20\quad21$
     
  3. $10\quad20$
     
  4. $11\quad20$

Consider the following C program:

int mystery(int a[]) {
    a[1] = -3;
    a = malloc(4 * sizeof(int));
    a[3] = -2;
    return a[2];
}
int main() {
    int array[] = {9, 8, 7, 6};
    array[2] = mystery(array);
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
        printf("%d ", array[i]);
}

What will be the output of the above program?

  1. $9$ $-3$ $0$ $6$
     
  2. $9$ $-3$ $7$ $-2$
     
  3. $9$ $-3$ $7$ $6$
     
  4. $9$ $8$ $0$  $6$

Consider the following C program:

Code 

void recurse(int n) {
    if (n != 0)
        recurse(n--);
    printf("%d ", n);
}

What will be the output or behaviour of the function if called as such recurse(5);?

  1. It prints the numbers from $5$ to $1$ in reverse order
     
  2. It prints nothing and causes a stack overflow
     
  3. It prints the numbers from $1$ to $5$ in same order
     
  4. It will lead to infinite recursion but no stack overflow

Consider the following functionfoo:

int foo(int a, int b) {
    if (a < b) {
        return b;
    }
    int diff = a - b;
    return foo(diff, b - 1) + foo(diff, b + 1);
}

Which one of the following statements best describes the function fooin the above code?

  1. Causes a runtime error because functions in C cannot be recursive.
     
  2. The function foois an example of an iterative method.
     
  3. The value of diff is shared across all recursive calls.
     
  4. Each recursive call to foo has its own local, temporary variable diff.

The following program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output of the program?
 

#include<stdio.h>
void rec(char str[], int n)
{
    if(n < 1)
        return;
    printf("%c", str[n - 1]);
    rec(str, n - 1);
}
int main(void)
{
    char str[] = "0123456789";
    rec(str, 5);
}
  1. $01234$
     
  2. $56789$
     
  3. $98765$
     
  4. $43210$

Code 

int main() {
    int *p;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
        p = malloc(sizeof(int) * 10);
        p[0] = i;
    }
    free(p);
    return 0;
}

Which of the following best describes the behaviour of the above program?

  1. No memory leak; p is freed properly
     
  2. Only the last allocated block is freed; the rest are leaked
     
  3. p becomes a dangling pointer before free()
     
  4. All 1000 allocations are freed correctly

Consider the following C function:

char* func(char* str) {
    char* ret = (char*) ((long*) ((int*) str + 2) + 1) + 3;
    return ret;
}

Assume the following:

sizeof(char) = 1 byte
sizeof(int) = 4 bytes
sizeof(long) = 8 bytes

Which of the following expressions is/are equivalent to the "ret" variable?

  1. str + $6$
     
  2. str + $19$
     
  3. &(str[$19$])
     
  4. str[$19$]

Code 

int main() {
    int i = 0, j, count = 0;
    for (j = -2; j <= 4; j++) {
        if ((j > 1) || (i++ && j == 0))
            count += j;
    }
    count += i;
    printf("%d\n", count);
    return 0;
}

What is the output of the program?

  1. $10$
     
  2. $12$
     
  3. $13$
     
  4. $15$

The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output the program produces?

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
    int x = 7;
    switch(x / 2)
    {
        case 1: printf("hangman\n");
                break;
        case 3: printf("pacman\n");
                break;
        case 7: printf("dave\n");
                break;
        default: printf("mario\n");
    }
}
  1. hangman
     
  2. pacman
     
  3. dave
     
  4. mario
